proposal: The Mandate recommends restoring and building on the first-term counter-China structure at USAID (the Clear Choice Executive Council, a senior coordinator and a review of proposed programs through a counter-China lens), assessing bilateral aid through national security interests and rewarding countries that resist Chinese debt diplomacy. It also calls for programs that counter specific Chinese efforts in strategic countries, ending funding to any partner that engages with Chinese entities directly or indirectly, and focusing the Bangkok-based regional mission for Asia on cross-border work against Chinese influence.

status_summary: USAID, the agency the text addresses, closed on 2025-07-01 and its remaining functions moved to the State Department, so the USAID-based Clear Choice structure and the Bangkok regional mission as described were not restored. In the successor structure, the one element found to be operative is funding for programs aimed at Chinese influence: the House and Senate committee summaries of the FY2026 law (Public Law 119-75, enacted 2026-02-03) both say it fully funds the Countering PRC Influence Fund, the House summary at $400 million, within more than $1.8 billion for the Indo-Pacific Strategy per the Senate summary. The Secretary of State described a proposed $2.9 billion America First Opportunity Fund as a tool against competitors such as China (testimony of 2025-05-21), but the enacted law set no dedicated amount for it. No counter-China review of all aid awards, no policy rewarding countries that resist Chinese debt diplomacy and no bar on partners that engage with Chinese entities was found, so the stage rests on one funding element and is held at the bottom of the in_progress band.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14169 paused foreign development assistance for a review of each program's alignment with US foreign policy.

The Secretary of State told a House appropriations subcommittee that the department was confronting Chinese influence and proposed an America First Opportunity Fund of about $2.9 billion usable against near-peer competitors such as China.
USAID officially closed and its remaining operations merged into the State Department.

Public Law 119-75 was enacted; the Senate Appropriations Committee's undated summary of the conference bill says it fully funds the Countering PRC Influence Fund within more than $1.8 billion for the Indo-Pacific Strategy.
The House Appropriations Committee's undated summary of the final bill says it fully funds the Countering PRC Influence Fund at $400 million.

title: Restore a counter-China architecture in foreign aid and screen aid through that lens
uncertainties: Neither committee summary prints a date; both are dated here to the enactment of P.L. 119-75 (2026-02-03, per CRS). The Senate summary gives no amount for the Countering PRC Influence Fund and the House summary gives $400 million; the enacted statutory text was not read, and the CRS report on FY2026 appropriations does not mention the fund. The fund existed before 2025 (reviewer background knowledge, not confirmed in a fetched source), so its FY2026 funding is a continuation rather than a new structure. No source was found on the fate of the Bangkok-based USAID Regional Development Mission for Asia after the 2025 closure; one reviewer search returned only regional commentary. No State document naming a Clear Choice framework or a counter-China review of aid was found. The State Department's Office of China Coordination (1 FAM 134, section text dated 2023; see related record c06-11) is a diplomatic office, not an aid screen, and the FAM section does not mention foreign assistance review. Executive Order 14169's review tested programs against US foreign policy in general, not a China-specific lens. The Mandate's ban on partners engaging with Chinese entities was not matched by any aid rule found. The bill number (H.R. 7148) and the 2026-02-03 enactment date were confirmed on GovInfo bill status data, and the enrolled law's table of contents on GovInfo lists Division F as the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026. The statutory line for the Countering PRC Influence Fund was not read because the GovInfo text as retrieved stops in Division A; the $400 million figure rests on the House committee summary of the final bill, which was re-read in this review.
